newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Franc falls after attack on German policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Franc falls after attack on German policy.

text.p: The franc tumbled on Thursday after a Bank of France council member launched a stinging attack on Germany's monetary policy and said it might be necessary to devalue the franc against the mark.

The franc slid more than a centime against the mark before retracing to trade at 3.3916 by late afternoon as economists said it was highly unlikely France would ditch its decade-old policy of keeping a stable currency tied to the German mark.
But it was still more than two-thirds of a centime down from the previous day.

The comments by Jean-Pierre Gerard, seen as a member of a minority camp on the council in favour of easier monetary policy, were seen as his own opinion by observers of the Bank, which left its rates unchanged at its regular repurchase tender.

But they served to stoke a growing row over France's strong franc policy triggered last week when former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a sharp devaluation to revive the flagging economy.

The government has strongly resisted calls for a weaker franc versus the mark. But one economist suggested the latest round of statements might be a behind-the-scenes campaign to pressure the Germans to cut rates and thus push up the dollar.

"They are not all loose cannons. I rather think that it may be (President Jacques) Chirac behind this, putting pressure on Germany, saying it is going to be very difficult here to continue on the road to monetary union," he said.

Gerard said a devaluation of the franc against the mark was undesirable but might be forced by German incomprehension about the problems its attachment to a powerful currency could have on the launch of the euro, the planned European currency.
Although Germany was satisfied with the current dollar rate, for France the correct parity would be around six francs per dollar -- compared with 5.20 francs now, Gerard said.
His statements followed those of another council member, Paul Marchelli, who cautioned this week against launching an overvalued single currency, particularly against the dollar.
Economists said the problem of a weak dollar was rearing its head as hopes faded that the United States would increase interest rates, which would help drive up its currency.
"I don't think it (the debate) will end with (a franc) devaluation but with a fall in German interest rates," said BFCE economist Francois Chevalier.
The market's nervousness has been exacerbated by concern over the expiration of the terms of two council members considered hawks on monetary policy at the end of the year.
The government's decision on renewing or replacing them is seen as a gauge of its commitment to the strong franc policy championed by Bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet.
Of the nine council members, the newspaper Liberation said the two whose terms expire are among the six hawks. Neither has given any indication of wanting to step down.
The other three, Gerard, Marchelli and Denise Flouzat, are seen as favouring a looser monetary policy.
The speakers of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the head of the Economic and Social Council put forward six candidates from whom the government will choose two.
Daily Le Monde has suggested Chirac, whose relations with Trichet have been chilly, might push for middle-of-the-road candidates with the ability to stand up to Trichet.
"When we have the two new members, they will be more or less doves and their first act will be to cut rates to the German level and then possibly lower," predicted one French economist.
He said the aim would not be to cut the French/mark parity but to put pressure on Germany to lower its rates to protect its economy and export industries.
